title: From Rs 18 Lakh Debt to Rs 2 Crore Sales: A Chole Bhature Miracle
excerpt: A tiny Chembur eatery was Rs 18 lakh in debt and about to close — then Abhishek Upmanyu's Instagram tip and Anushka Sharma's order for Virat Kohli turned Delhi Se into a four-outlet, Rs 2-crore-a-month brand.
body:
• Delhi Se, a 250-square-foot chole bhature outlet in Mumbai's Chembur, was Rs 18 lakh in debt and weeks away from shutting down in September 2022 — today it sells 3,000+ plates a day with monthly sales around Rs 2 crore.
  • The turnaround began with comedian Abhishek Upmanyu's Instagram recommendation, followed by Anushka Sharma ordering two plates of chole bhature for Virat Kohli and posting about it to her followers.
  • Owner Jaspal Singh Khalsa initially thought the call from Kohli's home was a prank — the plate cost Rs 120, less than the delivery cost from Chembur to Juhu.
  • The brothers now run four outlets across Mumbai and Navi Mumbai, soaking 125 kg of chhole daily — up from under 1 kg at their lowest.

The Phone Call That Sounded Like a Prank

When the phone rang at Delhi Se, a tiny chole bhature eatery in Mumbai's Chembur, owner Jaspal Singh Khalsa was certain someone was playing a trick on him. The caller — a woman — wanted two plates of chole bhature delivered to Juhu, and kept asking for his bank details to cover the extra delivery cost. "I told Mahinder, 'This woman is troubling me. She has called eight times and is asking for my bank details,'" Jaspal recalled, speaking about his brother and co-founder Mahinder Singh Khalsa. "Mahinder said, 'The account balance is already negative. There is hardly any money in it.'"

The caller was from Virat Kohli's home. The order was for the cricketer himself, who loves authentic Delhi-style flavours. The delivery was fixed for October 5, 2022 — and what followed rewrote the fate of a business that had been counting its final days.

"I said, 'Ma'am, please don't say things like that. Where is Virat Kohli and where am I — a small chhole bhature shop in Chembur?"

— Jaspal Singh Khalsa, co-owner of Delhi Se

Context & Background

The Khalsa brothers launched Delhi Se on October 15, 2021 — a modest 250-square-foot outlet with three tables and nine seats in Chembur's Camp area. Business started well but declined from January 2022. By September, they had accumulated around Rs 18 lakh in debt and were planning to close down. "From January, our sales started declining. By September 2022, we were planning to close the restaurant. We thought we would pay the last month's groceries and rent and then shut it down," Jaspal told Pinkvilla.

On September 11, the brothers prayed during Ganpati Visarjan for enough to manage an offering. Two days later, stand-up comedian Abhishek Upmanyu walked into the restaurant. He tried the chole bhature and recommended the place on his Instagram Story. The owners did not know who he was — but on September 14 and 15, walk-ins began rising. Upmanyu's recommendation reached Anushka Sharma, who had been searching for authentic Delhi-style chole bhature in Mumbai for Kohli.

Impact & Analysis

Anushka's Instagram post — celebrating "ekdum-Delhi-jaise-Chole-bhature in Mumbai" and crediting Upmanyu for the discovery — detonated the business. "After her post, there was a massive crowd at the restaurant. Within half an hour, such a huge crowd had gathered that we were completely blank," Jaspal said. Phones rang continuously, and police officials arrived after the crowd spilled outside.

The restaurant was not equipped for the surge. Customers ordered six or ten plates at a time. The brothers began asking neighbours to soak chhole at home. "Someone would order six plates, someone else would order 10. We didn't have enough stock. We didn't know this was going to happen," Jaspal said. Within three days, chhole preparation jumped from 8 kg to 100 kg.

Today, Delhi Se runs four outlets — in Chembur, Mulund, Andheri West and Vashi — and serves more than 3,000 plates of chole bhature every day. The brothers soak around 125 kg of chhole daily, which expands to nearly a tonne after cooking. Monthly sales, which had hovered at Rs 1–1.5 lakh while the restaurant struggled, are now claimed at around Rs 2 crore — roughly a 1,500-fold jump.

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, the Delhi Se story is about more than a viral restaurant — it is about the outsized economic power of Indian celebrity culture, something NRIs watch unfold in real time from Dubai, London and New Jersey. The Khalsa brothers' arc mirrors the diaspora's own small-business mythology: the Punjabi eatery that makes it against impossible odds. And there is a quieter resonance: Jaspal's disbelief at the call from Kohli's home — "where is Virat Kohli and where am I" — captures the gulf between India's celebrity economy and its street-level entrepreneurs, a gulf the diaspora bridges every time a hometown favourite gets a Bollywood shoutout.

What's Next

Delhi Se's challenge now is the classic post-viral problem: sustaining quality and service across four outlets once the Instagram glow fades. The brothers have so far kept the formula simple — one dish, done well — which gives them a better shot than most at durability. Whether they expand beyond Mumbai remains to be seen, but the brand has already become a case study in how a single endorsement can transform a balance sheet.
